claim: Fifteen participants (9 male, 6 female; all adults in the age group 18–32) participated in the experiments.
source: Fifteen participants (9 male, 6 female; all adults in the age group 18–32) participated in the experiments.
evidence: Directly stated demographic information about the study participants.

claim: Apart from two participants, all participants were unaware of the purpose of the study.
source: Apart from two participants, all participants were unaware of the purpose of the study.
evidence: Directly stated information about participant awareness.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board at Baylor College of Medicine.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Review Board at Baylor College of Medicine and all participants signed an approved consent form.
evidence: Directly stated ethical approval information.

claim: Participants used a joystick to control their linear and angular speed in a virtual environment based on visual and/or vestibular feedback.
source: Participants used an analog joystick (M20U9T-N82, CTI electronics, Stratford, CT) with two degrees of freedom and a circular displacement boundary to control their linear and angular speed in a virtual environment based on visual and/or vestibular feedback.
evidence: Directly stated description of the experimental setup.

claim: The visual stimulus was projected onto a large rectangular screen (width × height : 158 × 94 cm) positioned in front of the participant (77 cm from the rear of the head).
source: The visual stimulus was projected (Canon LV-8235 UST Multimedia Projector, Canon USA, Melville, NY) onto a large rectangular screen (width × height : 158 × 94 cm) positioned in front of the participant (77 cm from the rear of the head).
evidence: Directly stated information about the visual display setup.

claim: Participants wore headphones generating white noise to mask the auditory motion cues.
source: Participants wore headphones generating white noise to mask the auditory motion cues.
evidence: Directly stated experimental control measure.

claim: The ground plane was circular with a radius of 37.5 m.
source: The ground plane was circular with a radius of 37.5 m (near and far clipping planes at 5 and 3750 cm, respectively), with the participant positioned at its center at the beginning of each trial.
evidence: Directly stated parameter of the virtual environment.

claim: Each texture element was an isosceles triangle (base × height 5.95 × 12.95 cm) that was randomly repositioned and reoriented at the end of its lifetime.
source: Each texture element was an isosceles triangle (base × height 5.95 × 12.95 cm) that was randomly repositioned and reoriented at the end of its lifetime.
evidence: Directly stated description of visual stimulus elements.

claim: Each participant performed a total of about 1450 trials (mean ± standard deviation (SD): 1450 ± 224), split equally among the three sensory conditions.
source: Each participant performed a total of about 1450 trials (mean ± standard deviation (SD): 1450 ± 224), split equally among the three sensory conditions (mean ± SD – vestibular: 476 ± 71, visual: 487 ± 77, combined: 487 ± 77).
evidence: Directly stated experimental design information.

claim: Visual and vestibular steering cues allowed comparable accuracies only when participants controlled their acceleration.
source: Visual and vestibular steering cues allowed comparable accuracies only when participants controlled their acceleration, suggesting that vestibular signals, on their own, fail to support accurate path integration in the absence of sustained acceleration.
evidence: Directly stated finding from the study.

claim: Vestibular signals, on their own, fail to support accurate path integration in the absence of sustained acceleration.
source: Visual and vestibular steering cues allowed comparable accuracies only when participants controlled their acceleration, suggesting that vestibular signals, on their own, fail to support accurate path integration in the absence of sustained acceleration.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results.

claim: Performance in all conditions reflected a failure to fully adapt to changes in the underlying control dynamics.
source: Nevertheless, performance in all conditions reflected a failure to fully adapt to changes in the underlying control dynamics, a result that was well explained by a bias in the dynamics estimation.
evidence: Directly stated finding from the study.

claim: The failure to fully adapt to changes in control dynamics was well explained by a bias in the dynamics estimation.
source: Nevertheless, performance in all conditions reflected a failure to fully adapt to changes in the underlying control dynamics, a result that was well explained by a bias in the dynamics estimation.
evidence: Directly stated interpretation of results.

claim: An incorrect internal model of control dynamics affects navigation in volatile environments in spite of continuous sensory feedback.
source: This work demonstrates how an incorrect internal model of control dynamics affects navigation in volatile environments in spite of continuous sensory feedback.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion of the study.

claim: Path integration is a sensorimotor computation that can be used to infer latent dynamical states by integrating self-motion cues.
source: Path integration is a sensorimotor computation that can be used to infer latent dynamical states by integrating self-motion cues.
evidence: Directly stated definition based on established knowledge.

claim: In many past tasks, the motion was passive and/or restricted along predetermined, often one-dimensional (1D), trajectories.
source: First, in many tasks, the motion was passive and/or restricted along predetermined, often one-dimensional (1D), trajectories (Klatzky, 1998; Jürgens and Becker, 2006; Petzschner and Glasauer, 2011; Campos et al., 2012; Tramper and Medendorp, 2015).
evidence: Cited literature review of past experimental paradigms.

claim: Unlike time-varying actions that characterize navigation under natural conditions, participants' responses in past studies were often reduced to single, binary end-of-trial decisions.
source: Second, unlike time-varying actions that characterize navigation under natural conditions, participants' responses were often reduced to single, binary end-of-trial decisions (ter Horst et al., 2015; Chrastil et al., 2016; Koppen et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited literature review of past experimental paradigms.

claim: Studies that explored contributions of different sensory modalities in naturalistic settings failed to properly disentangle vestibular from motor cues generated during active locomotion.
source: Third, even studies that explored contributions of different sensory modalities in naturalistic settings failed to properly disentangle vestibular from motor cues generated during active locomotion (Kearns et al., 2002; Campos et al., 2010; Bergmann et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2017; Schubert et al., 2012; Péruch et al., 1999; Péruch et al., 2005).
evidence: Cited literature review identifying limitations in past research.

claim: Varying constraints have presumably resulted in inconsistent findings on the contribution of vestibular cues to path integration.
source: Furthermore, varying constraints have presumably resulted in inconsistent findings on the contribution of vestibular cues to path integration (Jürgens and Becker, 2006; Campos et al., 2010; ter Horst et al., 2015; Tramper and Medendorp, 2015; Koppen et al., 2019; Chrastil et al., 2019; Glasauer et al., 1994; Seidman, 2008).
evidence: Cited literature review identifying inconsistencies in past research.

claim: There is a tight link between path integration and spatial navigation on the one hand, and internal models and control dynamics on the other.
source: There is a tight link between path integration and spatial navigation on the one hand, and internal models and control dynamics on the other.
evidence: Directly stated conceptual framework.

claim: To accurately estimate self-motion, we rely not only on momentary sensory evidence but also on the knowledge of motion dynamics, that is, an internal model of the world.
source: To accurately estimate self-motion, we rely not only on momentary sensory evidence but also on the knowledge of motion dynamics, that is, an internal model of the world.
evidence: Directly stated theoretical framework.

claim: Knowledge of the dynamics makes the sensory consequences of actions predictable, allowing for more dexterous steering.
source: Knowledge of the dynamics makes the sensory consequences of actions predictable, allowing for more dexterous steering.
evidence: Directly stated theoretical principle.

claim: There is a large body of research focused on dynamics and adaptation for motor control.
source: However, although there is a large body of research focused on dynamics and adaptation for motor control (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994; Lackner and Dizio, 1994; Krakauer et al., 1999; Takahashi et al., 2001; Burdet et al., 2001; Kording et al., 2007; Berniker et al., 2010), studies of perceptual inference of latent dynamics during navigation have been limited.
evidence: Cited literature review of motor control research.

claim: Studies of perceptual inference of latent dynamics during navigation have been limited.
source: However, although there is a large body of research focused on dynamics and adaptation for motor control (Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994; Lackner and Dizio, 1994; Krakauer et al., 1999; Takahashi et al., 2001; Burdet et al., 2001; Kording et al., 2007; Berniker et al., 2010), studies of perceptual inference of latent dynamics during navigation have been limited.
evidence: Directly stated gap in the literature.

claim: Pioneering studies demonstrated participants' ability to reproduce arbitrary 1D velocity profiles.
source: Some pioneering studies demonstrated participants' ability to reproduce arbitrary 1D velocity profiles (Grasso et al., 1999; Israël et al., 1997), while more recent efforts showed that the history of linear (Petzschner and Glasauer, 2011) and angular (Prsa et al., 2015) displacements affects how participants process sensory input in the current trial.
evidence: Cited literature review of past research.

claim: The history of linear and angular displacements affects how participants process sensory input in the current trial.
source: Some pioneering studies demonstrated participants' ability to reproduce arbitrary 1D velocity profiles (Grasso et al., 1999; Israël et al., 1997), while more recent efforts showed that the history of linear (Petzschner and Glasauer, 2011) and angular (Prsa et al., 2015) displacements affects how participants process sensory input in the current trial.
evidence: Cited literature review of past research.

claim: False expectations about the magnitude of self-motion can have a drastic effect on path integration.
source: We previously observed that false expectations about the magnitude of self-motion can have a drastic effect on path integration (Lakshminarasimhan et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited previous work by the authors.

claim: A motion-cueing (MC) algorithm was designed to render self-motion stimuli according to a joystick control input of maintained accelerations while maintaining correspondence between visual (optic flow) and inertial cues.
source: To achieve this, we designed a motion-cueing (MC) algorithm to render self-motion stimuli according to a joystick control input of maintained accelerations while maintaining correspondence between visual (optic flow) and inertial cues.
evidence: Directly stated methodological innovation.

claim: The MC algorithm represents a departure from classical paradigms of navigation research in humans.
source: The development of the MC algorithm represents a departure from classical paradigms of navigation research in humans (Chrastil et al., 2019; Israël et al., 1996; Koppen et al., 2019; Seemungal et al., 2007; ter Horst et al., 2015), as it helps eliminate artificial constraints while still allowing for the isolation of different sensory contributions, most notably vestibular/somatosensory cues, during active, volitional, steering.
evidence: Directly stated comparison to past research methods.

claim: Participants' steering responses were biased (undershooting).
source: We found that participants' steering responses were biased (undershooting), and the biases were more prominent in the vestibular condition.
evidence: Directly stated finding from the study.

claim: The biases were more prominent in the vestibular condition.
source: We found that participants' steering responses were biased (undershooting), and the biases were more prominent in the vestibular condition.
evidence: Directly stated finding from the study.

claim: Steering biases were strongly modulated by the underlying control dynamics.
source: Furthermore, steering biases were strongly modulated by the underlying control dynamics.
evidence: Directly stated finding from the study.

claim: Inertial cues alone (as generated by motion cueing) lack the reliability to support accurate path integration in the absence of sustained acceleration.
source: These findings suggest that inertial cues alone (as generated by motion cueing) lack the reliability to support accurate path integration in the absence of sustained acceleration, and that an accurate internal model of control dynamics is needed to make use of sensory observations when navigating in volatile environments.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results.

claim: An accurate internal model of control dynamics is needed to make use of sensory observations when navigating in volatile environments.
source: These findings suggest that inertial cues alone (as generated by motion cueing) lack the reliability to support accurate path integration in the absence of sustained acceleration, and that an accurate internal model of control dynamics is needed to make use of sensory observations when navigating in volatile environments.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results.

claim: Participants sat on a motion platform in front of a screen displaying a virtual environment.
source: Participants sat on a motion platform in front of a screen displaying a virtual environment (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Stereoscopic depth cues were provided using polarizing goggles.
source: Stereoscopic depth cues were provided using polarizing goggles.
evidence: Directly stated experimental setup detail.

claim: On each trial, a circular target appeared briefly at a random location and participants had to navigate to the remembered target location in the virtual world using a joystick to control linear and angular self-motion.
source: On each trial, a circular target appeared briefly at a random location (drawn from a uniform distribution within the field of view; Figure 1B and C) and participants had to navigate to the remembered target location in the virtual world using a joystick to control linear and angular self-motion.
evidence: Directly stated task description with reference to figures.

claim: The virtual ground plane was defined visually by a texture of many small triangles which independently appeared only transiently.
source: The virtual ground plane was defined visually by a texture of many small triangles which independently appeared only transiently; they could therefore only provide optic-flow information and could not be used as landmarks.
evidence: Directly stated description of visual stimulus design.

claim: The ground plane triangles could only provide optic-flow information and could not be used as landmarks.
source: The virtual ground plane was defined visually by a texture of many small triangles which independently appeared only transiently; they could therefore only provide optic-flow information and could not be used as landmarks.
evidence: Directly stated design feature and its implication.

claim: The self-motion process evolved according to Markov dynamics, such that the movement velocity at the next time step depended only on the current joystick input and the current velocity.
source: The self-motion process evolved according to Markov dynamics, such that the movement velocity at the next time step depended only on the current joystick input and the current velocity (Materials and methods – Equation 1a).
evidence: Directly stated description of the control dynamics.

claim: The time constant of the filter varies across trials.
source: This input is lowpass filtered to mimic the existence of inertia. The time constant of the filter varies across trials (time constant τ).
evidence: Directly stated and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Maximum velocity also varies according to the time constant τ of each trial to ensure comparable travel times across trials.
source: In our framework, maximum velocity also varies according to the time constant τ of each trial to ensure comparable travel times across trials (see Materials and methods – Control Dynamics).
evidence: Directly stated design feature illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: τ = 0.6 s corresponds to velocity control.
source: The same joystick input (scaled by the corresponding maximum velocity for each τ) produces different velocity profiles for different time constants (τ = 0.6 s corresponds to velocity control; τ = 3 s corresponds to acceleration control; τ values varied randomly along a continuum across trials, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated parameter definition illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: τ = 3 s corresponds to acceleration control.
source: The same joystick input (scaled by the corresponding maximum velocity for each τ) produces different velocity profiles for different time constants (τ = 0.6 s corresponds to velocity control; τ = 3 s corresponds to acceleration control; τ values varied randomly along a continuum across trials, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated parameter definition illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: τ values varied randomly along a continuum across trials.
source: The same joystick input (scaled by the corresponding maximum velocity for each τ) produces different velocity profiles for different time constants (τ = 0.6 s corresponds to velocity control; τ = 3 s corresponds to acceleration control; τ values varied randomly along a continuum across trials, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated experimental design feature.

claim: The MC algorithm aims at controlling a platform such that the sum of inertial and gravitational acceleration experienced when sitting on the platform matches the linear acceleration experienced in the simulated virtual environment.
source: The MC algorithm aims at controlling a platform such that the sum of inertial and gravitational acceleration experienced when sitting on the platform (desired platform gravito-inertial acceleration [GIA], blue; the curve illustrates an example profile consisting of a single rectangular waveform) matches the linear acceleration experienced in the simulated virtual environment.
evidence: Directly stated description of the MC algorithm illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is an almost perfect match between visual acceleration and platform GIA.
source: Correspondence between visual acceleration and platform GIA (blue), measured independently from the MC algorithm using an inertial measurement unit mounted next to the participant's head. There is an almost perfect match between the two.
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The dashed line represents a conservative choice of the vestibular motion detection threshold according to the relevant literature (8 cm/s²).
source: The dashed line represents a conservative choice of the vestibular motion detection threshold according to the relevant literature (8 cm/s2; Kingma, 2005; MacNeilage et al., 2010; Zupan and Merfeld, 2008).
evidence: Cited threshold value illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Participants compared their stopping locations on each trial to the corresponding target locations, separately for each sensory condition.
source: We first compared the participants' stopping locations on each trial to the corresponding target locations, separately for each sensory condition.
evidence: Directly stated analysis method.

claim: There was substantial undershooting in the vestibular condition.
source: As shown with the example participant in Figure 2B and C, there was substantial undershooting in the vestibular condition, whereas performance was relatively unbiased under the combined and visual conditions (see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Performance was relatively unbiased under the combined and visual conditions.
source: As shown with the example participant in Figure 2B and C, there was substantial undershooting in the vestibular condition, whereas performance was relatively unbiased under the combined and visual conditions (see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Mean radial gain± standard deviation – vestibular: 0.76 ± 0.25, visual: 0.88 ± 0.23, combined: 0.85 ± 0.22.
source: These results were consistent across participants (Figure 2D, mean radial gain± standard deviation – vestibular: 0.76 ± 0.25, visual: 0.88 ± 0.23, combined: 0.85 ± 0.22, mean angular gain± standard deviation – vestibular: 0.79 ± 0.22, visual: 0.98 ± 0.14, combined: 0.95 ± 0.12), and no significant sex differences were observed (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative results illustrated in Figure 2D.

claim: Mean angular gain± standard deviation – vestibular: 0.79 ± 0.22, visual: 0.98 ± 0.14, combined: 0.95 ± 0.12.
source: These results were consistent across participants (Figure 2D, mean radial gain± standard deviation – vestibular: 0.76 ± 0.25, visual: 0.88 ± 0.23, combined: 0.85 ± 0.22, mean angular gain± standard deviation – vestibular: 0.79 ± 0.22, visual: 0.98 ± 0.14, combined: 0.95 ± 0.12), and no significant sex differences were observed (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative results illustrated in Figure 2D.

claim: No significant sex differences were observed in response gains.
source: These results were consistent across participants (Figure 2D, mean radial gain± standard deviation – vestibular: 0.76 ± 0.25, visual: 0.88 ± 0.23, combined: 0.85 ± 0.22, mean angular gain± standard deviation – vestibular: 0.79 ± 0.22, visual: 0.98 ± 0.14, combined: 0.95 ± 0.12), and no significant sex differences were observed (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Directly stated finding with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Both linear and angular components of control input had shorter duration in the vestibular condition.
source: The difference in response gain between modalities could be traced back to the control exerted by the subjects on the joystick. Both linear and angular components of control input had shorter duration in the vestibular condition (mean ± SEM of total area of joystick input across participants (a.u.): radial – vestibular: 5.62 ± 0.27, visual: 7.31 ± 0.33, combined: 7.07 ± 0.34; angular – vestibular: 2.39 ± 0.30, visual: 3.29 ± 0.42, combined: 3.79 ± 0.46), and produced smaller displacements, as summarized by the response gains (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated finding with quantitative data.

claim: Smaller time constants (velocity control) were associated with smaller response gains.
source: We found that smaller time constants (velocity control) were associated with smaller response gains (Figure 3A; Appendix 2—table 1).
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: This relationship was most pronounced in the vestibular condition, where larger time constants (acceleration control) resulted in better (closer to ideal) performance.
source: This relationship was most pronounced in the vestibular condition, where larger time constants (acceleration control) resulted in better (closer to ideal) performance (Figure 3, green; see Discussion).
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Control dynamics had a smaller but considerable effect on steering responses in the visual and combined conditions, with participants exhibiting modest overshooting (undershooting) when the time constant was large (small).
source: Control dynamics had a smaller but considerable effect on steering responses in the visual and combined conditions, with participants exhibiting modest overshooting (undershooting) when the time constant was large (small) (Figure 3A, cyan/purple).
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: A significant correlation was found between residual errors and the time constant across trials.
source: However, we found a significant correlation between residual errors and the time constant across trials (Figure 3B, C; Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Appendix 2—table 2, see Materials and methods; no significant sex differences were observed, and therefore are not investigated in subsequent analyses, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 3B and C.

claim: This correlation and the corresponding regression slopes were substantially higher in the vestibular condition.
source: This correlation and the corresponding regression slopes were substantially higher in the vestibular condition (mean Pearson's r ± SEM: radial component – vestibular: 0.52 ± 0.02, visual: 0.36 ± 0.03, combined: 0.37 ± 0.03; angular component – vestibular: 0.23 ± 0.02, visual: 0.23 ± 0.03, combined: 0.26 ± 0.03; see also Appendix 2—Tables 2 and 3).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative finding.

claim: For a given target distance, participants tended to travel further when the time constant was larger (acceleration control), indicating they did not fully adapt their steering control to the underlying dynamics.
source: Thus, for a given target distance, participants tended to travel further when the time constant was larger (acceleration control), indicating they did not fully adapt their steering control to the underlying dynamics.
evidence: Interpretation of the correlation results.

claim: The time constant contributed substantially to participants' response gain, albeit only by modulating the radial and angular distance dependence.
source: A partial correlation analyses revealed that the time constant contributed substantially to participants' response gain, albeit only by modulating the radial and angular distance dependence (Appendix 2—table 4; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; see Materials and methods – Equation 4).
evidence: Directly stated finding from partial correlation analysis.

claim: The contribution of the time constant-dependent term was much greater for the vestibular condition.
source: Again, the contribution of the time constant-dependent term was much greater for the vestibular condition (Figure 3D), especially for the radial distance (p-values of difference in coefficient values across modalities obtained by a paired t-test – radial: vestibular vs. visual: p < 10–4 , vestibular vs. combined: p < 10–4; angular: vestibular vs. visual: p = 0.016, vestibular vs. combined: p = 0.013).
evidence: Directly stated finding with statistical significance illustrated in Figure 3D.

claim: All three independent analyses revealed that control dynamics did substantially influence the steering response gain, exposing participants' failure to adapt their steering to the underlying dynamics.
source: While perfect adaptation should lead to response gain that is independent of control dynamics, all three independent analyses revealed that control dynamics did substantially influence the steering response gain, exposing participants' failure to adapt their steering to the underlying dynamics.
evidence: Summary of findings from multiple analyses.

claim: Adaptation was lowest for the vestibular condition; in contrast, for the visual and combined conditions, the response gain was less affected indicating greater compensation when visual information was available.
source: Adaptation was lowest for the vestibular condition; in contrast, for the visual and combined conditions, the response gain was less affected indicating greater compensation when visual information was available.
evidence: Summary comparison of adaptation across conditions.

claim: The true response gains in the vestibular condition were much closer to the no-adaptation null case, compared to visual/combined conditions.
source: We found that the true response gains in the vestibular condition were much closer to the no-adaptation null case, compared to visual/combined conditions (Figure 3E).
evidence: Directly stated finding from null-case simulation illustrated in Figure 3E.

claim: This finding was more prominent in the radial component of the response gain.
source: Interestingly, this finding was more prominent in the radial component of the response gain (Figure 3E insets), consistent with our earlier observations of a stronger influence of the dynamics on the radial component of the responses.
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 3E insets.

claim: Participants do tend to brake more for higher time constants, but this effect is weaker in the vestibular condition.
source: Indeed, participants do tend to brake more for higher time constants, but this effect is weaker in the vestibular condition (Figure 4 and inset).
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 4.

claim: Correlations between the time constant and cumulative braking were significant in all sensory conditions.
source: Nevertheless, correlations between the time constant and cumulative braking (total area below zero linear control input) were significant in all sensory conditions (mean Pearson's r ± SEM – vestibular: 0.20 ± 0.03, visual: 0.62 ± 0.04, combined: 0.57 ± 0.04; p-values of Pearson's r difference from zero – vestibular: p = 10−5, visual: p < 10−7, combined: p < 10−7).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative finding with statistical significance.

claim: Behavior in the vestibular condition is minimally influenced by the dynamics (i.e. smaller modulation of control input by the time constant, as shown by the cumulative braking).
source: Overall, it appears that behavior in the vestibular condition is minimally influenced by the dynamics (i.e. smaller modulation of control input by the time constant, as shown by the cumulative braking).
evidence: Summary interpretation of braking behavior.

claim: When optic flow is available, participants are more flexible in adjusting their control.
source: When optic flow is available, however, participants are more flexible in adjusting their control.
evidence: Summary interpretation of control adjustment.

claim: Accumulating sensory noise over an extended time (~10 s) would lead to a large uncertainty in the participant's beliefs about their position, causing them to undershoot.
source: We have shown previously that accumulating sensory noise over an extended time (~10 s) would lead to a large uncertainty in the participant's beliefs about their position, causing them to undershoot (Lakshminarasimhan et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited previous work by the authors.

claim: The exact amount of undershooting depends both on the reliability of self-motion cues, which determines the instantaneous uncertainty in the self-motion estimate, and on travel duration, which governs how much uncertainty is accumulated while navigating to the target.
source: The exact amount of undershooting depends both on the reliability of self-motion cues, which determines the instantaneous uncertainty in the self-motion estimate, and on travel duration, which governs how much uncertainty is accumulated while navigating to the target.
evidence: Directly stated theoretical framework.

claim: Recent findings ascribe uncertainty accumulation to noise in the velocity input.
source: With recent findings ascribing uncertainty accumulation to noise in the velocity input (Stangl et al., 2020), the observed differences in navigation performance across sensory modalities can be readily attributed to greater measurement noise (lower reliability) in vestibular signals.
evidence: Cited recent research.

claim: The observed differences in navigation performance across sensory modalities can be readily attributed to greater measurement noise (lower reliability) in vestibular signals.
source: With recent findings ascribing uncertainty accumulation to noise in the velocity input (Stangl et al., 2020), the observed differences in navigation performance across sensory modalities can be readily attributed to greater measurement noise (lower reliability) in vestibular signals.
evidence: Interpretation based on cited research.

claim: Stimulus parameters were adjusted to ensure that the average travel time and average velocity were similar across different control dynamics.
source: We adjusted stimulus parameters to ensure that the average travel time and average velocity were similar across different control dynamics (Materials and methods – Equation 1.2-1.10), however, we found that travel duration and average velocity depend weakly on the time constant in some participants.
evidence: Directly stated experimental design feature.

claim: Travel duration and average velocity depend weakly on the time constant in some participants.
source: We adjusted stimulus parameters to ensure that the average travel time and average velocity were similar across different control dynamics (Materials and methods – Equation 1.2-1.10), however, we found that travel duration and average velocity depend weakly on the time constant in some participants.
evidence: Directly stated finding.

claim: Simulations suggest that both dependencies are a consequence of maladaptation to the dynamics rather than a cause of the observed effect of the dynamics on the responses.
source: Simulations suggest that both dependencies are a consequence of maladaptation to the dynamics rather than a cause of the observed effect of the dynamics on the responses.
evidence: Directly stated interpretation from simulations.

claim: The dependence is stronger in the vestibular condition where there is less adaptation to the dynamics, agreeing with our simulations.
source: Interestingly, the dependence is stronger in the vestibular condition where there is less adaptation to the dynamics, agreeing with our simulations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Difference in velocity profiles is an unlikely explanation since their expected effect on the participants' responses (undershoot) is the opposite of the observed effect of the control dynamics (overshooting tendency).
source: Difference in velocity profiles is also an unlikely explanation since their expected effect on the participants' responses (undershoot) is the opposite of the observed effect of the control dynamics (overshooting tendency; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Directly stated reasoning illustrated in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Unlike the effect of sensory modality on response gain, neither instantaneous nor accumulated differences in the uncertainty can fully account for the influence of control dynamics, that is, the time constant.
source: Consequently, unlike the effect of sensory modality on response gain, neither instantaneous nor accumulated differences in the uncertainty can fully account for the influence of control dynamics, that is, the time constant.
evidence: Summary interpretation of findings.

claim: The data are well explained by strong prior expectations about motion dynamics that cause a bias in estimating the time constant.
source: Instead, we will now show that the data are well explained by strong prior expectations about motion dynamics that cause a bias in estimating the time constant.
evidence: Directly stated interpretation to be demonstrated.

claim: To optimally infer movement velocity, one must combine sensory observations with the knowledge of the time constant.
source: From a normative standpoint, to optimally infer movement velocity, one must combine sensory observations with the knowledge of the time constant.
evidence: Directly stated normative principle.

claim: Misestimating the time constant would produce errors in velocity estimates, which would then propagate to position estimates, leading control dynamics to influence response gain.
source: Misestimating the time constant would produce errors in velocity estimates, which would then propagate to position estimates, leading control dynamics to influence response gain (Figure 5A, middle-right).
evidence: Directly stated theoretical prediction illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: In the absence of performance-related feedback at the end of the trial, participants would be unaware of this discrepancy, wrongly believing that the actual trajectory was indeed the intended one.
source: However, in the absence of performance-related feedback at the end of the trial, participants would be unaware of this discrepancy, wrongly believing that the actual trajectory was indeed the intended one.
evidence: Directly stated theoretical reasoning.

claim: Participants' imperfect adaptation to changes in control dynamics could be a consequence of control dynamics misestimation.
source: In other words, participants' imperfect adaptation to changes in control dynamics could be a consequence of control dynamics misestimation.
evidence: Directly stated hypothesis.

claim: The correlation between residual error and time constant was indeed significantly smaller when these errors were computed using the subjective (believed) rather than real stopping location.
source: In all cases, we observed that the correlation between residual error and time constant was indeed significantly smaller when these errors were computed using the subjective (believed) rather than real stopping location (Figure 5B).
evidence: Directly stated finding from model validation illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: Subjective residual errors were completely uncorrelated with the time constant suggesting that the Bayesian model is a good model of participants' beliefs.
source: In fact, subjective residual errors were completely uncorrelated with the time constant suggesting that the Bayesian model is a good model of participants' beliefs, and that the apparent influence of control dynamics on behavioral performance was entirely because participants misestimated the time constant of the underlying dynamics.
evidence: Directly stated interpretation of model validation results.

claim: The apparent influence of control dynamics on behavioral performance was entirely because participants misestimated the time constant of the underlying dynamics.
source: In fact, subjective residual errors were completely uncorrelated with the time constant suggesting that the Bayesian model is a good model of participants' beliefs, and that the apparent influence of control dynamics on behavioral performance was entirely because participants misestimated the time constant of the underlying dynamics.
evidence: Directly stated conclusion from model validation.

claim: In the vestibular condition, all participants consistently misestimated τ, exhibiting a substantial regression toward the mean.
source: In the vestibular condition, all participants consistently misestimated τ, exhibiting a substantial regression toward the mean (Figure 6A, green).
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: This effect was much weaker in the visual condition.
source: This effect was much weaker in the visual condition. Only a few participants showed relatively flat estimates, with the majority showing smaller departures from ideal estimates (dashed line).
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: The data for the combined condition followed a similar trend, with properties between those in the visual and vestibular conditions.
source: The data for the combined condition followed a similar trend, with properties between those in the visual and vestibular conditions (Figure 6A, purple).
evidence: Directly stated finding illustrated in Figure 6A.

claim: The better control adaptation in the visual and combined conditions is due to participants' improved estimates of the time constant when optic flow was available.
source: These results suggest that the better control adaptation in the visual and combined conditions shown in Figure 3 is due to participants' improved estimates of the time constant when optic flow was available.
evidence: Interpretation of model parameter results.

claim: The ratio was close to one for the visual and combined conditions, suggesting equal weighting of prior and likelihood.
source: Notably, the ratio was close to one for the visual and combined conditions, suggesting equal weighting of prior and likelihood.
evidence: Interpretation of model parameter results.

claim: Participants' estimate of the control dynamics in the vestibular condition was plagued by a combination of strong prior and weak likelihood, which explains the much stronger regression toward the mean.
source: Thus, participants' estimate of the control dynamics in the vestibular condition was plagued by a combination of strong prior and weak likelihood, which explains the much stronger regression toward the mean in Figure 6A.
evidence: Summary interpretation of model parameters.

claim: The performance of the static and dynamic prior models was comparable in all conditions, for both distance and angle, suggesting that a static prior is adequate in explaining the participants' behavior on this task.
source: The performance of the static and dynamic prior models was comparable in all conditions, for both distance and angle, suggesting that a static prior is adequate in explaining the participants' behavior on this task (Figure 7; light vs. dark bars).
evidence: Directly stated model comparison result illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: When updating the prior in the dynamic model, the weighting of the previous-trial prior received significantly more weight in the vestibular condition.
source: In line with our expectations, when updating the prior in the dynamic model, the weighting of the previous-trial prior received significantly more weight in the vestibular condition (in the range of [0,1]; mean prior weights ± SEM– vestibular: 0.93 ± 0.03, visual: 0.48 ± 0.10, combined: 0.61 ± 0.09; p-value of paired weight differences obtained by bootstrapping – vestibular vs. visual: p = 10–5 , vestibular vs. combined: p = 4 · 10–4; visual vs. combined: p = 0.08).
evidence: Directly stated finding from dynamic prior model with statistical significance.

claim: The comparable goodness of models with static and dynamic priors suggest that sensory observations were not too reliable to cause rapid changes in prior expectations during the course of the experiment.
source: The comparable goodness of models with static and dynamic priors suggest that sensory observations were not too reliable to cause rapid changes in prior expectations during the course of the experiment.
evidence: Interpretation of model comparison results.

claim: For visual and combined conditions, the fixed τ model not only fails to minimize the correlations but, in fact, strongly reverses it, for both distance and angle.
source: For visual and combined conditions, the fixed τ model not only fails to minimize the correlations but, in fact, strongly reverses it, for both distance (left) and angle (right).
evidence: Directly stated finding from fixed τ model illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Model performance was only comparable in the vestibular condition, where the average correlation of the fixed τ model was contained within the 95% confidence intervals of the static prior Bayesian model.
source: Model performance was only comparable in the vestibular condition, where the average correlation of the fixed τ model (F) was contained within the 95% confidence intervals (CI) of the static prior Bayesian model (S), for both distance and angle (distance – F: mean Pearson's correlation coefficient ρ = 0.03, S: 95% CI of Pearson's correlation coefficient ρ = [–0.10 0.25]; angle – F: mean Pearson's correlation coefficient ρ = –0.01, S: 95% CI of Pearson's correlation coefficient ρ = [–0.12 0.15]).
evidence: Directly stated quantitative model comparison result.

claim: The carry-over strategy does not seem likely since it fails to explain away a large part of the correlation between the radial component of the subjective residual errors and the time constant.
source: The carry-over strategy does not seem likely since it fails to explain away a large part of the correlation between the radial component of the subjective residual errors and the time constant (compare rightmost cyan/purple bars with gray bars; p-values of paired t-test between radial correlation coefficients – current vestibular vs. previous visual trial estimation: p=0.006, current vestibular vs. previous combined trial estimation: p=0.02; p-values of paired t-test between angular correlation coefficients – current vestibular vs. previous visual trial estimation: p=0.008, current vestibular vs. previous combined trial estimation: p = 0.71).
evidence: Directly stated finding from carry-over model illustrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The sensory feedback control model predicts a much stronger dependence of the responses on the dynamics compared to our data.
source: However, this model predicts a much stronger dependence of the responses on the dynamics compared to our data, and characteristics of the predicted control input differ significantly from the actual control (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated finding from sensory feedback control model illustrated in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Our results suggest that optic flow, but not vestibular signals, primarily contributes to inferring the latent velocity dynamics.
source: Overall, our results suggest that optic flow, but not vestibular signals, primarily contributes to inferring the latent velocity dynamics.
evidence: Summary conclusion from model comparisons.

claim: Participants can navigate using different sensory cues and changes in the control dynamics affect their performance.
source: We showed that human participants can navigate using different sensory cues and that changes in the control dynamics affect their performance.
evidence: Summary of main findings.

claim: Participants can path integrate to steer toward a remembered target location quite accurately in the presence of optic flow.
source: Specifically, we showed that participants can path integrate to steer toward a remembered target location quite accurately in the presence of optic flow.
evidence: Summary of main findings.

claim: Inertial (vestibular/somatosensory) cues generated by motion cueing alone lacked the reliability to support accurate path integration, leading to substantially biased responses under velocity control.
source: In contrast, inertial (vestibular/somatosensory) cues generated by motion cueing alone lacked the reliability to support accurate path integration, leading to substantially biased responses under velocity control.
evidence: Summary of main findings.

claim: Performance was also influenced by the changing control dynamics in all sensory conditions.
source: Performance was also influenced by the changing control dynamics in all sensory conditions.
evidence: Summary of main findings.

claim: Because control dynamics were varied on a trial-by-trial basis, sensory cues were crucial for inferring those dynamics.
source: Because control dynamics were varied on a trial-by-trial basis, sensory cues were crucial for inferring those dynamics.
evidence: Directly stated interpretation of experimental design.

claim: The observed responses are consistent with estimates of the control dynamics that were biased toward the center of the experimental distribution.
source: We used probabilistic inference models to show that the observed responses are consistent with estimates of the control dynamics that were biased toward the center of the experimental distribution.
evidence: Summary of modeling results.

claim: This was particularly strong under the vestibular condition such that the response gain substantially increased as the motion dynamics tended toward acceleration control.
source: This was particularly strong under the vestibular condition such that the response gain substantially increased as the motion dynamics tended toward acceleration control.
evidence: Summary of modeling results.

claim: Although control dynamics were correlated across trials, our models showed that participants did not take advantage of those correlations to improve their estimates.
source: Although control dynamics were correlated across trials, our models showed that participants did not take advantage of those correlations to improve their estimates.
evidence: Summary of modeling results.

claim: In the paradigm used here, participants actively controlled linear and angular motion, allowing us to study multisensory path integration in two dimensions with few constraints.
source: In the paradigm used here, participants actively controlled linear and angular motion, allowing us to study multisensory path integration in two dimensions with few constraints.
evidence: Directly stated description of the experimental paradigm.

claim: This paradigm was made possible by the development of an MC algorithm to render visual and vestibular cues either synchronously or separately.
source: This paradigm was made possible by the development of an MC algorithm to render visual and vestibular cues either synchronously or separately.
evidence: Directly stated methodological contribution.

claim: Findings from past studies that evaluate the contributions of different sensory modalities to self-motion perception may be more limited in generalizing to real-world navigation.
source: As a result, findings from past studies that evaluate the contributions of different sensory modalities to self-motion perception (Chrastil et al., 2019; Israël et al., 1996; Koppen et al., 2019; Seemungal et al., 2007; ter Horst et al., 2015) may be more limited in generalizing to real-world navigation.
evidence: Interpretation comparing current work to past research.

claim: At least in humans, navigation is driven primarily by visual cues under conditions of near-constant travel velocity (velocity control).
source: Our results show that, at least in humans, navigation is driven primarily by visual cues under conditions of near-constant travel velocity (velocity control).
evidence: Summary interpretation of results.

claim: This dominance of vision suggests that the reliability of the visual cues is much higher than vestibular cues (as generated by our platform).
source: This dominance of vision suggests that the reliability of the visual cues is much higher than vestibular cues (as generated by our platform), as corroborated by the data from the combined condition in which performance resembles the visual condition.
evidence: Interpretation of results.

claim: The vestibular system is mainly sensitive to acceleration, exhibiting higher sensitivity to higher-frequency motion compared to the visual system.
source: This makes sense because the vestibular system is mainly sensitive to acceleration, exhibiting higher sensitivity to higher-frequency motion compared to the visual system (Karmali et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited established knowledge about the vestibular system.

claim: The vestibular system may only be reliable when motion is dominated by acceleration.
source: Consequently, it may only be reliable when motion is dominated by acceleration.
evidence: Inference based on cited knowledge.

claim: This interpretation is further supported by the observation that participants' vestibular performance was a lot less biased in the regime of acceleration joystick control, where accelerations are prolonged during navigation.
source: This interpretation is further supported by the observation that participants' vestibular performance was a lot less biased in the regime of acceleration joystick control, where accelerations are prolonged during navigation.
evidence: Interpretation supported by experimental observations.

claim: Experimental constraints in past navigation studies have also precluded examining the influence of control dynamics.
source: Experimental constraints in past navigation studies have also precluded examining the influence of control dynamics.
evidence: Directly stated limitation of past research.

claim: The importance of accurately inferring control dynamics, which are critical for predicting the sensory consequences of actions, has largely been studied in the context of limb control and motor adaptation.
source: In fact, the importance of accurately inferring control dynamics, which are critical for predicting the sensory consequences of actions, has largely been studied in the context of limb control and motor adaptation (Burdet et al., 2001; Kording et al., 2007; Krakauer et al., 1999; Lackner and Dizio, 1994; Shadmehr and Mussa-Ivaldi, 1994; Takahashi et al., 2001).
evidence: Cited literature review of motor control research.

claim: We provide evidence for the importance of accurately inferring control dynamics in the context of path integration and spatial navigation.
source: Here, we provide evidence for the importance of accurately inferring control dynamics in the context of path integration and spatial navigation.
evidence: Directly stated contribution of the current work.

claim: Although participants were not instructed to expect changes in the latent dynamics and received no feedback, they nevertheless partly adapted to those dynamics while exhibiting a bias toward prior expectations about these dynamics.
source: Although participants were not instructed to expect changes in the latent dynamics and received no feedback, we showed that they nevertheless partly adapted to those dynamics while exhibiting a bias toward prior expectations about these dynamics.
evidence: Summary of findings.

claim: This biased estimation of control dynamics led to biased path integration performance.
source: This biased estimation of control dynamics led to biased path integration performance.
evidence: Directly stated causal interpretation.

claim: This result is analogous to findings about the effect of changing control dynamics in motor control: first, adaptation to the dynamics happens even in the absence of performance-related feedback and, second, this adaptation relies on prior experience and leads to systematic errors when knowledge of the dynamics is inaccurate.
source: This result is analogous to findings about the effect of changing control dynamics in motor control: first, adaptation to the dynamics happens even in the absence of performance-related feedback (Batcho et al., 2016; Lackner and Dizio, 1994) and, second, this adaptation relies on prior experience (Arce et al., 2009) and leads to systematic errors when knowledge of the dynamics is inaccurate (Körding et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited analogous findings from motor control literature.

claim: Participants try to exploit the additional information that the dynamics contain about their self-motion in order to achieve the desired displacement.
source: Thus, participants try to exploit the additional information that the dynamics contain about their self-motion in order to achieve the desired displacement.
evidence: Interpretation of participant behavior.

claim: A Bayesian estimator with a static prior over the dynamics sufficiently explained participants' beliefs in our data, while results were comparable with a dynamic prior that was updated at every trial.
source: A Bayesian estimator with a static prior over the dynamics sufficiently explained participants' beliefs in our data, while results were comparable with a dynamic prior that was updated at every trial.
evidence: Summary of modeling results.

claim: This could be attributed to the structure of the random walk of the control dynamics across trials, as a static prior is not as computationally demanding and potentially more suitable for fast changes in the time constant.
source: This could be attributed to the structure of the random walk of the control dynamics across trials, as a static prior is not as computationally demanding and potentially more suitable for fast changes in the time constant.
evidence: Interpretation of modeling results.

claim: These Bayesian models attempt to explain behavior in an optimal way given the task structure.
source: These Bayesian models attempt to explain behavior in an optimal way given the task structure.
evidence: Directly stated description of modeling approach.

claim: Alternative suboptimal models (fixed estimate, carry-over estimate, sensory feedback model) failed to explain behavior successfully, especially when optic flow was available.
source: Meanwhile, alternative suboptimal models (fixed estimate, carry-over estimate, sensory feedback model) failed to explain behavior successfully, especially when optic flow was available.
evidence: Summary of model comparison results.

claim: These results strongly favor underlying computations within the context of optimality in the presence of optic flow.
source: These results strongly favor underlying computations within the context of optimality in the presence of optic flow.
evidence: Interpretation of model comparison results.

claim: Task performance was substantially worse in the vestibular condition, in a manner suggesting that vestibular inputs from motion cueing lack the reliability to precisely estimate control dynamics on individual trials.
source: Task performance was substantially worse in the vestibular condition, in a manner suggesting that vestibular inputs from motion cueing lack the reliability to precisely estimate control dynamics on individual trials.
evidence: Summary interpretation of results.

claim: The vestibular system could still facilitate inference by integrating trial history to build expectations about their statistics.
source: Nevertheless, the vestibular system could still facilitate inference by integrating trial history to build expectations about their statistics.
evidence: Directly stated hypothesis.

claim: The mean of the prior distribution over the dynamics fit to data was very close to the mean of the true sampled distribution, suggesting that even if within-trial vestibular observations are not sufficient, participants possibly combine information about the dynamics across trials to construct their prior beliefs.
source: Consistent with this, the mean of the prior distribution over the dynamics fit to data was very close to the mean of the true sampled distribution, suggesting that even if within-trial vestibular observations are not sufficient, participants possibly combine information about the dynamics across trials to construct their prior beliefs.
evidence: Interpretation of model parameter results.

claim: This is consistent with the findings of Prsa et al., 2015, where vestibular cues were used to infer an underlying pattern of magnitude of motion across trials.
source: This is consistent with the findings of Prsa et al., 2015, where vestibular cues were used to infer an underlying pattern of magnitude of motion across trials.
evidence: Cited related research.

claim: The measurement of the dynamics in Prsa et al., 2015 substantially differs from ours: here, motion dynamics are inferred using self-motion cues within each trial whereas in Prsa et al., 2015, the dynamics were inferred by integrating observations about the magnitude of the displacement across trials.
source: However, the measurement of the dynamics in that study substantially differs from ours: here, motion dynamics are inferred using self-motion cues within each trial whereas in Prsa et al., 2015, the dynamics were inferred by integrating observations about the magnitude of the displacement across trials.
evidence: Comparison to cited research.

claim: If vestibular cues can in fact support inference of dynamics – as recent findings suggest in eye-head gaze shifts – a common processing mechanism could be shared across sensory modalities.
source: If vestibular cues can in fact support inference of dynamics – as recent findings suggest in eye-head gaze shifts (Sağlam et al., 2014) – a common processing mechanism could be shared across sensory modalities.
evidence: Cited research and speculation about mechanisms.

claim: This finding highlights the importance of incorporating estimates of the control dynamics in models of self-motion perception and path integration.
source: Overall, this finding highlights the importance of incorporating estimates of the control dynamics in models of self-motion perception and path integration.
evidence: Summary conclusion about modeling implications.

claim: Restrictions of our motion platform limited the range of velocities that could be tested, allowing only for relatively small velocities.
source: Note that restrictions of our motion platform limited the range of velocities that could be tested, allowing only for relatively small velocities (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated limitation of the study.

claim: Trial durations were long, but the motion platform also restricted total displacement, so we could not test larger target distances.
source: Consequently, trial durations were long, but the motion platform also restricted total displacement, so we could not test larger target distances.
evidence: Directly stated limitation of the study.

claim: Our results in the visual and combined conditions are comparable for similar travel times to previous studies with larger velocities.
source: We previously studied visual path integration with larger velocities and our results in the visual and combined conditions are comparable for similar travel times (as trials exceeded durations of 10 s, undershooting became more prevalent; Lakshminarasimhan et al., 2018).
evidence: Comparison to previous work by the authors.

claim: It is unclear how larger velocities (and accelerations) would affect participants' performance (especially under the vestibular condition) and whether the present conclusions are also representative of the regime of velocities not tested.
source: However, it is unclear how larger velocities (and accelerations) would affect participants' performance (especially under the vestibular condition) and whether the present conclusions are also representative of the regime of velocities not tested.
evidence: Directly stated limitation and uncertainty.

claim: The design of the MC algorithm allowed us to circumvent the issues associated with the physical limitations of the platform to a large degree.
source: The design of the MC algorithm allowed us to circumvent the issues associated with the physical limitations of the platform to a large degree.
evidence: Directly stated methodological advantage.

claim: This was achieved in part by exploiting the tilt/translation ambiguity and substituting linear translation with tilt.
source: This was achieved in part by exploiting the tilt/translation ambiguity and substituting linear translation with tilt (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Directly stated methodological approach.

claim: High-frequency accelerations, as those found at movement onset, generated tilts that briefly exceeded the tilt-detection threshold of the semicircular canals.
source: However, high-frequency accelerations, as those found at movement onset, generated tilts that briefly exceeded the tilt-detection threshold of the semicircular canals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly stated limitation illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Although the duration of suprathreshold stimulation was very small, we cannot exclude the possibility that the perceived tilt affected the interpretation of vestibular inputs.
source: Although the duration of suprathreshold stimulation was very small, we cannot exclude the possibility that the perceived tilt affected the interpretation of vestibular inputs.
evidence: Directly stated limitation and uncertainty.

claim: Participants may not attribute tilt to linear translation, hence underestimating their displacement, which would lead to overshooting to compensate for the lack of perceived displacement, which is not what we observed in our experiment.
source: For example, participants may not attribute tilt to linear translation, hence underestimating their displacement. This, however, would lead to overshooting to compensate for the lack of perceived displacement,which is not what we observed in our experiment.
evidence: Hypothetical explanation ruled out by data.

claim: Another potential explanation for the poor vestibular performance could be that participants perceive tilt as a conflicting cue with respect to their expected motion or visual cues, in which case participants would only use the vestibular inputs to a small extent if at all.
source: Another potential explanation for the poor vestibular performance could be that participants perceive tilt as a conflicting cue with respect to their expected motion or visual cues. In that case, participants would only use the vestibular inputs to a small extent if at all.
evidence: Hypothetical explanation for findings.

claim: Manipulating vestibular inputs (e.g. gain, noise manipulations) in future experiments, either alone or in conjunction with visual cues, would offer valuable insights on two fronts: first, to help clarify the efficiency of our MC algorithm and its implications on the design of driving simulators in the future, and second, to precisely quantify the contribution of vestibular cues to path integration in natural settings.
source: Manipulating vestibular inputs (e.g. gain, noise manipulations) in future experiments, either alone or in conjunction with visual cues, would offer valuable insights on two fronts: first, to help clarify the efficiency of our MC algorithm and its implications on the design of driving simulators in the future, and second, to precisely quantify the contribution of vestibular cues to path integration in natural settings.
evidence: Directly stated suggestions for future research.

claim: For the sake of simplicity, we modeled each trial's control dynamics as a single measurement per trial when, in reality, participants must infer the dynamics over the course of a trial using a dynamic process of evidence accumulation.
source: For the sake of simplicity, we modeled each trial's control dynamics as a single measurement per trial when, in reality, participants must infer the dynamics over the course of a trial using a dynamic process of evidence accumulation.
evidence: Directly stated simplification in the modeling approach.

claim: Although we were able to explain the experimental findings of the influence of control dynamics on steering responses with our model, this approach could be expanded into a more normative framework using hierarchical Bayesian models to infer subjective position estimates by marginalizing over possible control dynamics.
source: Although we were able to explain the experimental findings of the influence of control dynamics on steering responses with our model, this approach could be expanded into a more normative framework using hierarchical Bayesian models (Mathys et al., 2011) to infer subjective position estimates by marginalizing over possible control dynamics.
evidence: Directly stated suggestion for future modeling work.

claim: One interesting question is whether providing feedback would eliminate the inference bias of the control dynamics estimation and future studies should explicitly test this hypothesis.
source: One interesting question is whether providing feedback would eliminate the inference bias of the control dynamics estimation and future studies should explicitly test this hypothesis.
evidence: Directly stated suggestion for future research.

claim: It would be interesting to jointly introduce sensory conflict and manipulate sensory reliability to study dynamic multisensory integration such that sensory contributions during navigation can be better disentangled.
source: Furthermore, it would be interesting to jointly introduce sensory conflict and manipulate sensory reliability to study dynamic multisensory integration such that sensory contributions during navigation can be better disentangled.
evidence: Directly stated suggestion for future research.

claim: Although it has been shown that cue combination takes place during path integration, previous studies have had contradicting results regarding the manner in which body-based and visual cues are combined.
source: Although it has been shown that cue combination takes place during path integration (Tcheang et al., 2011), previous studies have had contradicting results regarding the manner in which body-based and visual cues are combined (Campos et al., 2010; Chrastil et al., 2019; Koppen et al., 2019; Petrini et al., 2016; ter Horst et al., 2015).
evidence: Cited literature review identifying inconsistencies.

claim: Since visual and vestibular signals differ in their sensitivity to different types of motion, the outcomes of their integration may depend on the self-motion stimuli employed.
source: Since visual and vestibular signals differ in their sensitivity to different types of motion (Karmali et al., 2014), the outcomes of their integration may depend on the self-motion stimuli employed.
evidence: Cited knowledge and inference about cue integration.

claim: Combined with hierarchical models of self-motion inference that considers the control dynamics, it is possible to develop an integrated, multi-level model of navigation, while constraining dramatically the hypothesized brain computations and their neurophysiological correlates.
source: Combined with hierarchical models of self-motion inference that considers the control dynamics, it is possible to develop an integrated, multi-level model of navigation, while constraining dramatically the hypothesized brain computations and their neurophysiological correlates.
evidence: Directly stated suggestion for future theoretical work.

claim: The MC took advantage of this ambiguity to replace linear acceleration by tilt.
source: The MC took advantage of this ambiguity to replace linear acceleration by tilt.
evidence: Directly stated methodological approach.

claim: As long as the rotation that induced this simulated acceleration was slow enough, the motion felt subjectively was a linear acceleration.
source: As long as the rotation that induced this simulated acceleration was slow enough, the motion felt subjectively was a linear acceleration.
evidence: Directly stated perceptual consequence of the MC algorithm.
